# Introduction

> What Umbra is, how it works in one minute, and where to go next in these docs.

Umbra pins small, sharp, true-black widgets to the Windows desktop. They sit under every window, never steal focus, stay visible with <kbd>Win</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd> and start with Windows.

A widget is a folder with a `widget.json` and a web page (HTML, CSS and JavaScript). Umbra's host app, written in C# on .NET 10, opens each enabled widget in its own borderless WebView2 window and pins it to the desktop. The host knows nothing about any particular widget, so anyone can build one.

## Why it feels different

- **It stays where it belongs.** Widget windows are owned by the desktop shell and kept at the bottom of the window stack, so your apps always cover them.
- **It's sharp.** Windows are opaque true black with corners and a hairline border drawn by Windows itself, so text keeps full ClearType quality. On an OLED screen the black pixels are simply off, and each card seems to float on your wallpaper.
- **It's safe.** A widget can only reach the HTTPS hosts it declares. The host blocks everything else. An update that asks for new access waits for your OK, and a widget can start a local program only if it declared that exact command and you approved it.
- **It's private.** No account, no tracking. Settings, widget data and logs stay in `%APPDATA%\Umbra`; the one thing Umbra reports is an anonymous +1 when you install a catalog widget, and you can turn that off.
- **It's scriptable.** The `umbractl` command line and a built-in [MCP server](/umbra/docs/automate/mcp/) let scripts and AI agents arrange widgets, take screenshots and write new widgets.

## Where to go next

| You want to… | Read |
|---|---|
| Install Umbra and add your first widgets | [Install](/umbra/docs/get-started/install/), then [Quickstart](/umbra/docs/get-started/quickstart/) |
| Arrange, theme and tune your desktop | [Using Umbra](/umbra/docs/using/settings/) |
| Build a widget | [Your first widget](/umbra/docs/widgets/first-widget/) and the [SDK reference](/umbra/docs/widgets/sdk-reference/) |
| Script Umbra or connect an AI agent | [Automate](/umbra/docs/automate/overview/) |
| Work on the app itself | [Internals](/umbra/docs/internals/architecture/) |

:::tip[For AI agents]
Every page has a **View as Markdown** link, and [`llms.txt`](/umbra/llms.txt) lists them all. [`llms-full.txt`](/umbra/llms-full.txt) is the whole manual in one file.
:::

## Requirements

Windows 10 version 1809 or later, or Windows 11. Umbra uses the WebView2 runtime, which ships with current Windows; the installer tells you if it's missing. A Linux version is in progress ([#172](https://github.com/AmineChr54/umbra/issues/172)).

Umbra is free and open source under the MIT license.

---

# Install

> Install Umbra with the per-user installer or as a portable copy, build it from source, and uninstall it.

## Installer (recommended)

1. Download **`UmbraSetup.exe`** from the [latest release](https://github.com/AmineChr54/umbra/releases/latest).
2. Run it. It installs for your user only, so there's no admin prompt, and asks whether Umbra should start with Windows.
3. Umbra starts in the **tray** (the notification area next to the clock). Click the tray icon, or open Umbra from the Start menu, to open **Settings**.
4. Go to **Browse** and install your first widgets.

The installer puts the app in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Umbra` and adds `umbractl` to your `PATH`. Your data lives in `%APPDATA%\Umbra`:

| Path | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `settings.json` | All settings: general options, each widget's options, position and size |
| `widgets\` | Widgets you installed from Browse or wrote with an agent |
| `data\<id>.json` | Data each widget saved with `umbra.store` (1 MB cap per widget) |
| `themes\` | Installed themes |
| `trash\` | Widgets you removed in Settings, kept 7 days for **Undo** |
| `umbra.log` | The log (Settings → Data & privacy → Open log) |

Umbra checks GitHub once a day for a new version and downloads it in the background. A dot on the tray icon means an update is ready; see [Updates](/umbra/docs/using/updates/).

:::note[SmartScreen]
If Windows shows "Windows protected your PC", click **More info** → **Run anyway**. New releases build up SmartScreen reputation over time.
:::

## Portable copy

Download `Umbra-<version>-portable.zip` from the [releases page](https://github.com/AmineChr54/umbra/releases), unzip it anywhere and run `Umbra.exe`.

The `portable.txt` file next to `Umbra.exe` keeps all data (settings, widgets, logs and the WebView2 cache) in a `data` folder beside the exe. Portable copies:

- don't start with Windows and don't update themselves (Settings → About shows a download link instead),
- run alongside an installed copy without sharing anything,
- work with the `umbractl.exe` next to them, which finds the same copy.

To make any folder portable, create an empty `portable.txt` next to `Umbra.exe`. See [Portable mode](/umbra/docs/internals/portable-mode/) for how it works.

## winget

A winget package (`AmineChr54.Umbra`) is prepared with every release but not yet published to the winget repository. Until then, use the installer.

## Build from source

You need the .NET 10 SDK, Node.js and Inno Setup 6.

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/AmineChr54/umbra
cd umbra
powershell -File build.ps1          # both exes + installer -> dist/UmbraSetup-<version>.exe
dotnet run --project src/Umbra      # or run from source (quit the installed Umbra first)
```

See [Dev setup and tests](/umbra/docs/internals/dev-setup/) for the full workflow.

## Uninstall

Open **Settings → Apps → Installed apps** in Windows, find **Umbra** and choose **Uninstall**. Your data in `%APPDATA%\Umbra` stays, so a reinstall picks up where you left off. Delete that folder to remove everything. For a portable copy, quit Umbra from the tray and delete its folder.

---

# Quickstart

> From a fresh install to an arranged desktop in five minutes, plus your first command-line and widget experiments.

This walks you from a fresh [install](/umbra/docs/get-started/install/) to a desktop you've arranged yourself.

## 1. Add widgets

Click the Umbra icon in the tray (the notification area next to the clock), or open Umbra from the Start menu, to open **Settings**. Go to **Browse** and click **Install** on a few widgets: Clock, Weather and To Do are a good start. Each card lists exactly what the widget can reach (for example `api.open-meteo.com`, or **No network access**), so you know what you're installing.

New widgets appear on your desktop at once, each in its default position.

## 2. Arrange them

Open the tray menu and choose **Edit mode** (or turn it on from **My widgets**). Every unlocked widget gets an outline and a corner handle:

- **Drag** a widget to move it. Guide lines show when it lines up with an edge, a center or a neighbour. Hold <kbd>Shift</kbd> while dragging to skip snapping.
- **Drag the corner** (or hold <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> and scroll) to resize. Widgets zoom like a web page, so text stays sharp.
- **Click a widget** to select it, then nudge it with the arrow keys: 1 px, or 10 px with <kbd>Shift</kbd>.

A small **Editing widgets · Snap · Done** pill appears at the top of each monitor that has widgets. Click **Done** (or press <kbd>Esc</kbd> on a clicked widget) to leave edit mode. See [Arranging widgets](/umbra/docs/using/arranging-widgets/) for everything edit mode can do.

## 3. Make them yours

In **My widgets**, each widget has its own card: change its options (a city, a currency, a time format), its size, its opacity, and when it should be visible. Under **General** you can set the accent color, corner radius and fonts, and **Themes** switches the whole look in one click. All changes apply live.

## 4. Peek and show the desktop

Press <kbd>Win</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd>: your widgets stay where they are. To bring them above your apps for a few seconds without moving anything, use **Peek**. Assign hotkeys for it, for edit mode, for refresh and for show/hide in **Settings → Hotkeys** ([details](/umbra/docs/using/hotkeys-peek-layouts/)).

## 5. Try the command line

The installer puts `umbractl` on your `PATH`. Every command prints JSON, and starts Umbra in the background if it isn't running:

```powershell
umbractl list                          # your widgets, options and positions
umbractl install sp500                 # install from the catalog
umbractl set sp500 symbol ^IXIC        # follow the Nasdaq instead; applies instantly
umbractl configure sp500 --scale 1.5   # 150 % size
umbractl capture sp500 shot.png        # a PNG of just that widget
```

The [command reference](/umbra/docs/automate/cli/) lists every command.

## 6. Build your own

```powershell
umbractl new my-widget
```

This creates a working widget in `%APPDATA%\Umbra\widgets\my-widget` and shows it on your desktop. Edit its files, run `umbractl reload`, and follow [Your first widget](/umbra/docs/widgets/first-widget/).

:::tip
If something looks wrong, **Settings → About → Copy diagnostics** gives you a block you can paste into a bug report, and **safe mode** turns community widgets off without deleting anything. See [Troubleshooting](/umbra/docs/using/troubleshooting/).
:::

---

# FAQ

> Short answers about how Umbra works, what it can access, and how it compares to other desktop widget tools.

## Does Umbra work with Win+D?

Yes. Each widget window is owned by the desktop shell and kept at the bottom of the window stack, so <kbd>Win</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd> leaves your widgets visible and every app covers them. See [Desktop pinning](/umbra/docs/internals/desktop-pinning/).

## Will a widget steal focus while I type?

No. Widget windows never activate themselves. A widget gets the keyboard only right after you press the mouse on it (for example to type in a text field). A widget can't pull focus on its own.

## Is it safe to install community widgets?

Each widget runs in a sandbox. It can load only Umbra's own virtual hosts and the HTTPS hosts it declares in its `widget.json`; every other request is blocked by the app. An update that asks for new access (more hosts, notifications, media, commands) waits for your approval, and a widget can start a local program only if it declared that exact command and you approved it. Every catalog widget is also reviewed in a pull request. Details: [Sandbox and permissions](/umbra/docs/widgets/sandbox/) and the [security model](/umbra/docs/internals/security/).

## Does Umbra collect data?

No account and no tracking. Settings, widget data and logs stay in `%APPDATA%\Umbra` on your PC. The only network traffic Umbra itself makes is a daily check for a new release on GitHub, the widget catalog and its install counts when you open **Browse**, one anonymous +1 for a catalog widget when you install it (just the widget's id; turn it off in **Data & privacy**), and the requests widgets make to hosts they declare. **Settings → Data & privacy** shows what each widget can reach and store.

## Why are the windows opaque black, not transparent?

On Windows, translucent layered windows lose ClearType, so text gets blurrier. Umbra's windows are opaque true black with DWM-drawn rounded corners and a hairline border, which keeps full text quality. On an OLED display black pixels are off, so each card still looks like it floats on your wallpaper.

## How is this different from Rainmeter?

Rainmeter skins are described in its own format and drawn on translucent windows. Umbra widgets are ordinary web pages (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) in WebView2, so anything you can build for the web works, with a small SDK for refresh, options, saved data, notifications and media. The original Rainmeter skin of this project is still in [`extras/rainmeter`](https://github.com/AmineChr54/umbra/tree/main/extras/rainmeter).

## Does it use a lot of memory or battery?

Each widget is a WebView2 window. Umbra pauses widgets while the PC is locked or the display is off, stretches refresh intervals 4x on Windows Energy Saver (you can turn that off), and can hide widgets during fullscreen apps and games. Keep the number of widgets reasonable on low-end machines.

## Can I run two copies of one widget?

Yes: **My widgets → Add another copy**. Each copy has its own options, position, size and saved data, so you can show the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq side by side. See [Copies and tab groups](/umbra/docs/using/copies-and-tab-groups/).

## Where is my data?

In `%APPDATA%\Umbra`: `settings.json`, `widgets\` (installed widgets), `data\<id>.json` (what each widget saved), `themes\`, `trash\` and `umbra.log`. Portable copies keep all of it in a `data` folder next to `Umbra.exe`. Use **Data & privacy → Export backup** (or `umbractl backup <file>`) to save it.

## How do I update Umbra and its widgets?

Umbra checks GitHub daily, downloads updates in the background and shows a dot on the tray icon when one is ready; install it from the tray menu or **Settings → About**. Widget updates appear on **Browse**. See [Updates](/umbra/docs/using/updates/).

## Does it run on macOS or Linux?

Not yet. Umbra needs Windows 10 version 1809 or later, or Windows 11. A Linux version is in progress, see [Linux port](/umbra/docs/internals/linux-port/).

## Can an AI agent build widgets for me?

Yes. Run `claude mcp add umbra -- umbractl mcp` (or point any MCP client at `umbractl mcp`) and ask for the widget you want. The agent reads the authoring guide, writes the widget, takes a screenshot of just that widget and fixes what it sees. See [MCP server](/umbra/docs/automate/mcp/).

## I found a bug. What do I do?

Open **Settings → About → Copy diagnostics**, then use the issue link on the same page (it pre-fills your version) and paste the diagnostics. For security problems, read [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/AmineChr54/umbra/blob/main/SECURITY.md) instead.

---

# Settings tour

> A page-by-page tour of Umbra's Settings window, with keyboard shortcuts and where each setting is stored.

Open Settings from the tray icon, from the Start menu, or by launching Umbra a second time (a second launch opens Settings in the running copy). The window reopens where you left it: size, monitor, maximized state and last page.

## Pages

| Page | What it does |
|---|---|
| **General** | Start with Windows, refresh interval, animations, appearance (corner radius, border, accent color or the Windows accent, interface font and size, light text, reduce transparency) and advanced options (log level, developer mode, GPU, startup delay, proxy). |
| **My widgets** | Turn each widget on or off, edit its options, size and opacity, lock it, give it its own refresh interval, schedule when it shows, add another copy or reset its position. Also where you start edit mode and approve or revoke widget commands. |
| **Layouts** | Save the arrangement of your widgets under a name, then apply, rename or delete it. Layouts can switch automatically when you dock or undock. |
| **Browse** | The community catalog: install, update or remove widgets in one click. Each card shows the hosts, notifications, media and commands a widget asks for. |
| **Themes** | Install community themes and switch between them live. |
| **Hotkeys** | Global shortcuts for edit mode, refresh, show/hide, peek and Settings. |
| **Data & privacy** | What each widget can reach and store, recent blocked requests, backup and restore, reset, and safe mode. |
| **About** | Version, update status (with release notes once after an update), source link, **Copy diagnostics** for bug reports and pre-filled issue links. |

## Keyboard

- <kbd>Esc</kbd> closes Settings.
- <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>F</kbd> or <kbd>/</kbd> jumps to the Browse search.
- <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>1</kbd> to <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>7</kbd> switch pages.
- The arrow keys move through the sidebar and the refresh interval.

Switches and buttons have names for screen readers.

## Changes apply live

There is no Save button. Changing a setting updates widgets immediately, and `settings.json` in your data folder is written for you. Settings that need a restart say so: the proxy and hardware acceleration.

## The tray menu

The tray icon's tooltip shows the widget count and whether edit mode or safe mode is on. A dot on the icon means an Umbra update is ready. The menu opens Settings, toggles edit mode, opens the data folder, restarts Umbra, and offers **Undo** for a widget copy you just removed.

## The same settings from a script

Everything in Settings is also available from [`umbractl`](/umbra/docs/automate/cli/) and the [MCP server](/umbra/docs/automate/mcp/), for example `umbractl general --refresh 120` and `umbractl configure sp500 --scale 1.5`.

---

# Arranging widgets

> Edit mode, snapping, resizing and zooming, locking, and moving widgets between monitors.

## Edit mode

Turn edit mode on from the tray menu, from **My widgets**, with a [hotkey](/umbra/docs/using/hotkeys-peek-layouts/), or with `umbractl edit-mode on`. Unlocked widgets get an outline and a corner handle, and Umbra covers them with an overlay so presses move them instead of clicking inside the page.

| Action | How |
|---|---|
| Move | Drag the widget |
| Resize | Drag the right edge, bottom edge or corner handle |
| Zoom | Hold <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> and scroll over the widget |
| Select | Click it (stronger outline); it also takes the keyboard |
| Nudge | Arrow keys: 1 px, or 10 px (one grid step when snapping is on) with <kbd>Shift</kbd> |
| Snap | Hold <kbd>Shift</kbd> while dragging (default); or set `--snap-mode always` or General > Advanced > Snapping so widgets always snap and Shift skips it |
| Leave | **Done** on the pill, or <kbd>Esc</kbd> on a clicked widget |

A small **Editing widgets · Snap · Done** pill is drawn at the top of each monitor that has widgets. It has the snap switch and the **Done** button. Edit mode is off again after a restart.

## Size and zoom

Each widget has a design size from its `widget.json`. You can resize freely from **50 %** to **300 %** of it on each side. Widgets zoom like a web page, so text and charts stay sharp. A widget made only wider or taller keeps its zoom and gets more room; one made bigger on both sides is drawn larger. Set the size exactly in **My widgets**, or with `umbractl configure <id> --scale 1.5`.

## Snapping

While you drag in edit mode, widgets snap to a grid, to the edges and centers of other widgets, and to a gap you choose, and guide lines show what you're aligning to. Configure it in **General** or from the command line:

```powershell
umbractl general --snap-grid 20      # grid in px (0 = off)
umbractl general --snap-edges on     # snap to other widgets' edges and centers
umbractl general --snap-gap 12       # px kept between neighbours (0 = touch)
umbractl general --snap off          # master switch (also on the edit-mode pill)
umbractl general --snap-mode always  # shift (default) = snap only while Shift is held; always = Shift skips snapping
```

## Locking

A locked widget doesn't move, resize or zoom, even in edit mode. Lock widgets once you're happy with the layout: **My widgets → Lock**, the right-click menu, or `umbractl lock <id>`.

## Positions and monitors

Positions are screen coordinates in physical pixels. A widget remembers which monitor it was on, keeps its offset, and survives monitor changes. Move one to another monitor with `umbractl configure <id> --monitor 2` (a number from `umbractl status`, or `primary`). **Reset position** puts a widget back at its default.

## The right-click menu

Right-click a widget for **Refresh, Options** (opens Settings on its card), **Lock, Edit mode, Hide** and **Add another copy**. Extra copies can be removed from the menu, with **Undo** in the tray menu. A widget that handles right-click itself keeps its own menu; <kbd>Shift</kbd>+right-click always opens Umbra's.

## Save the arrangement

Once it looks right, [save it as a layout](/umbra/docs/using/hotkeys-peek-layouts/#layouts) so you can bring it back after a dock or undock.

---

# Hotkeys, peek and layouts

> Global hotkeys, the peek gesture, and named layouts that follow your monitor setup.

## Hotkeys

Global hotkeys work from any app. None are set by default. Assign them in **Settings → Hotkeys** or from the command line.

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| `edit-mode` | Turns [edit mode](/umbra/docs/using/arranging-widgets/) on or off |
| `refresh-all` | Asks every widget to fetch fresh data now |
| `toggle-widgets` | Shows or hides all widgets |
| `peek` | Raises widgets above other windows for a few seconds |
| `open-settings` | Opens Settings |

```powershell
umbractl hotkeys                          # read the current hotkeys and their status
umbractl hotkeys edit-mode Ctrl+Alt+E     # set one
umbractl hotkeys edit-mode off            # clear one
umbractl hotkeys reset                    # clear all
```

Each hotkey reports a status: `active`, `off`, or `failed` with the reason, for example when another app already uses that combination.

## Peek

Peek raises your widgets above every other window for a few seconds, then puts them back at the bottom, without moving or focusing anything. It's the quick way to glance at your widgets without closing your apps. The duration is 5 seconds by default; change it with `umbractl general --peek-seconds 1-60`, or run it directly:

```powershell
umbractl peek          # default duration
umbractl peek 10       # ten seconds
```

Peek does nothing while widgets are hidden.

## Layouts

A layout is a saved arrangement: the position, size and enabled state of every widget. Options and saved data are never touched by a layout.

```powershell
umbractl layouts                      # list
umbractl layouts save Work            # store the current arrangement
umbractl layouts apply Work           # switch to it, live
umbractl layouts rename Work Docked
umbractl layouts delete Docked
```

Saving pins the layout to the monitor setup you saved it on. An opt-in setting makes Umbra apply the matching layout automatically when you dock or undock. Layouts are managed on the **Layouts** page of Settings, where you can also rename and delete them.

## Hide during fullscreen

**General → Hide widgets during fullscreen apps and games** (`umbractl general --hide-fullscreen on`) keeps widgets out of the way while a fullscreen window is in the foreground.

---

# Copies and tab groups

> Run a widget more than once with separate options, and stack several widgets in one spot with tab groups.

## Copies

**My widgets → Add another copy** (or `umbractl add-instance <id>`) runs the same widget a second time. A copy has an id like `sp500#2`, and that id works anywhere a widget id does.

Each copy is a separate window with its own:

- options (follow the S&P 500 in one and the Nasdaq in the other),
- enabled and locked state, position and size,
- saved data (`umbra.store`).

```powershell
umbractl add-instance sp500                 # creates sp500#2
umbractl set sp500#2 symbol ^IXIC
umbractl remove-instance sp500#2            # removes the copy and its data
```

The first copy can't be removed, only disabled. Removing an extra copy from the right-click menu offers **Undo** in the tray menu for a short while.

## Tab groups

A tab group lets several widgets share one spot on the screen with only one visible at a time. A hover tab strip switches between them, and the visible tab takes over the group's shared position and size.

```powershell
umbractl groups                              # list groups
umbractl groups create todo "Work"           # a new group, starting from the widget copy "todo"
umbractl groups join <group> clock           # add a widget copy to a group
umbractl groups activate <group> clock       # show one
umbractl groups next <group>                 # also: previous
umbractl groups cycle <group> 30             # rotate every 30 s (5-3600; off to stop)
umbractl groups rename <group> "Focus"
umbractl groups icon clock rocket            # tab icon: a bundled name, or `default`
umbractl groups reorder <group> clock 0
umbractl groups leave clock                  # remove a widget from its group
umbractl groups delete <group>               # ungroup; the widgets stay
```

`<group>` is the group id that `umbractl groups` prints.

Tab icons come from the widget's own `icon.png` (64×64, light grey on transparent) or from the bundled icon set, which you pick in Settings or with `umbractl groups icon`. Your choice wins over the widget's icon.

---

# Visibility and refresh rules

> Control when each widget is shown, how opaque it is, and how often it updates, including what Umbra does while the PC is locked or on battery saver.

Everything here is per widget (and per copy) unless noted, in **Settings → My widgets**, from the right-click menu, or with `umbractl configure`.

## When a widget is shown

| Setting | What it does | `umbractl configure` flag |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Show or hide the widget | `--enabled on\|off` (or `enable`/`disable <id>`) |
| Start hidden | Opens hidden until you show it | `--start-hidden on\|off` |
| Show only between | A daily time range | `--show-from 08:00 --show-to 18:00` (`--show-from always` clears it) |
| Show only on AC power | Hide on battery | `--show-on-ac on` |
| Opacity | Dim a widget, `0.2` to `1` | `--opacity 0.8` (or `opaque`) |

```powershell
umbractl configure clock --show-from 08:00 --show-to 18:00 --show-on-ac on
umbractl configure clock --opacity 0.6
```

**All widgets at once:** the `toggle-widgets` [hotkey](/umbra/docs/using/hotkeys-peek-layouts/) shows or hides every widget, and **General → Hide widgets during fullscreen apps and games** (`umbractl general --hide-fullscreen on`) hides them while a fullscreen app is in the foreground.

## How often a widget updates

Widgets that fetch data refresh on an interval. The default is set in **General** (30 to 600 seconds), and each widget can have its own:

```powershell
umbractl general --refresh 120                 # default for all widgets
umbractl configure sp500 --refresh 300         # this widget only (or `default`)
umbractl refresh                               # fetch fresh data now, for all (or one id)
```

Umbra also refreshes widgets after the PC resumes from sleep, when the network comes back and after a long lock, at most once every 10 seconds.

## Automatic slowing and pausing

- **Locked or display off:** widgets are paused. They get one refresh when the PC is unlocked or the display is back on.
- **Windows Energy Saver:** refresh intervals are stretched 4x while it's on. Turn this off with `umbractl general --energy-saver off`.
- **Animations:** off in **General**, or follow the Windows reduced-motion preference. Calm animation speed doubles animation durations.

Widget authors read these from `umbra.settings` (`paused`, `energySaver`, `refreshSeconds`), see the [JavaScript API](/umbra/docs/widgets/javascript-api/).

---

# Appearance and themes

> Change corner radius, accent color, fonts, borders and motion for every widget, and switch community themes live.

Umbra styles widgets through design tokens, so one setting restyles every widget that follows them. Changes apply live.

## Appearance settings

In **Settings → Appearance → Customize colors, text and size**:

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Corner radius** | `default`, `sharp` or `round`. Overrides the theme's `--radius-s/m/l`. |
| **Accent color** | A color of your choice, or **Match Windows accent**, which follows the system accent live (lightened if it is too dark for black). Empty uses the theme's accent. |
| **Interface font and size** | Sets `--font` and `--font-scale`. Widgets that size text in `em`/`rem` follow the scale. |
| **Light text** | Brighter `--text*` colors. |
| **Window border** | On or off, and its color. |
| **Reduce transparency** | Solid `--line*` and `--accent-soft`, opaque windows. |
| **Animation speed** | `normal`, `calm` (animation durations doubled) or `off`. Windows' reduced-motion preference is respected. |
| **Size of new widgets** | The starting scale for new widgets, 0.5 to 3. |

The same settings from a terminal:

```powershell
umbractl general --corner-radius round --animation-speed calm
umbractl set-general --accent "#ff7a59" --light-text on --ui-font Consolas --font-scale 1.1 --border off --reduce-transparency on
```

## Themes

A theme restyles every widget at once: surfaces, lines, text, accent, up/down colors and corner radii. Switch in **Settings → Appearance**, or:

```powershell
umbractl themes                  # installed themes and the community catalog
umbractl install-theme ember     # install from the catalog
umbractl theme ember             # switch, live (`umbractl theme default` for Umbra Black)
umbractl remove-theme ember
```

"Umbra Black" is the built-in default. The catalog ships Ember, Glacier and Mono. Themes are **data only**: a list of named color and radius tokens with strict value checks, never code, so a theme can't load anything. Your own appearance settings (accent, corner radius, font) are applied on top of the theme.

Widgets that set `"themeable": false` in their manifest keep their own look. To make a theme, see [Build a theme](/umbra/docs/themes/build-a-theme/).

## Windows contrast themes

When Windows has a contrast theme on, Umbra maps the tokens to system colors and ignores themes and accents, so widgets stay readable. Widget authors can read about it in the [styling guide](/umbra/docs/widgets/styling/).

---

# Data, privacy and backups

> What Umbra stores and sends, the Data and privacy page, backup and restore, the trash, and safe mode.

## What Umbra stores

Everything lives in `%APPDATA%\Umbra` (or the `data` folder next to `Umbra.exe` in a [portable copy](/umbra/docs/internals/portable-mode/)). The environment variable `UMBRA_DATA_DIR` overrides the location.

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `settings.json` | Settings, per-widget options, positions, layouts, hotkeys, active theme |
| `widgets\<id>\` | Installed community and agent-written widgets |
| `data\<id>.json` | What a widget saved with `umbra.store` (1 MB cap per widget) |
| `themes\<id>\` | Installed themes |
| `approvals.json` | Which widget commands you approved |
| `trash\<id>-<timestamp>\` | Widgets removed in Settings, kept 7 days for **Undo** |
| `umbra.log` | The log |

## What Umbra sends

Umbra has no account and doesn't track you. Its own network traffic is limited to:

1. a daily check for a new release on GitHub (turn it off with `umbractl general --updates off`),
2. the widget and theme catalog when you open **Browse** or **Themes**, plus the install counts Browse shows,
3. one anonymous +1 for a catalog widget when you install it from the catalog: the request is just the widget's id, with no
   user or machine id, no version and nothing about your PC, and updates or file installs aren't counted. The Umbra relay
   keeps only the total per widget. Turn it off with **Count my widget installs** in **Data & privacy**; that also stops
   Browse from loading the counts,
4. requests that widgets make to hosts they declared in their `widget.json`.

This website counts page views the same way: the page's path and the referring site's name, no cookie, no id, and
nothing at all when your browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

A widget cannot reach anything it didn't declare; the app blocks the rest. See [Sandbox and permissions](/umbra/docs/widgets/sandbox/).

## The Data & privacy page

**Settings → Data & privacy** shows, for every widget:

- the hosts it can reach and the local commands it declares (and whether you approved them),
- how much data it has saved, with a **Delete data** button,
- recent blocked requests (a request to a host the widget didn't declare),
- how many times its renderer crashed.

It also has **Export** and **Import backup**, **Open data folder** and **Open log**, **Reset everything**, and **safe mode**. The same read-only report is `umbractl privacy [id]`.

## Backup and restore

```powershell
umbractl backup C:\Backups\umbra.json     # settings, layouts, theme, hotkeys and widget data
umbractl restore C:\Backups\umbra.json    # validated before anything is replaced
```

A backup **never includes command approvals**, so after a restore you approve widget commands again. The trash is not part of backups either.

## Removing widgets

- **Settings → Remove** moves the widget folder, its data and its settings (for every copy) to the trash for 7 days, with an **Undo** button on the toast. The trash is purged at startup after 7 days. (Undo does not bring back the working folders of `permissions.commands` runs.)
- `umbractl remove <id>` and the MCP `remove_widget` delete a widget and its data for good, with no undo.

## Safe mode

Safe mode turns community widgets off without deleting anything, so you can find a misbehaving one. Turn it on from **Data & privacy**, with `umbractl safe-mode on`, or start Umbra with `Umbra.exe --safe`. It isn't saved: the next normal start restores everything.

---

# Updates

> How Umbra updates itself, how widget and theme updates work, and why an update can wait for your approval.

## Updating Umbra

Umbra checks GitHub once a day for a new release. When one is found it downloads the installer in the background and verifies it, then shows a **dot on the tray icon**. Install it from the tray menu or **Settings → About**.

Installing closes Umbra, runs the installer silently with a small dark progress window, and starts the new version. After an update, **About** shows the release notes once.

```powershell
umbractl check-update       # is a newer version out? (it never installs one)
umbractl general --updates off    # stop the daily check
```

What Umbra will install is restricted: the installer must be an HTTPS download from this project's GitHub releases and named `UmbraSetup-<version>.exe`. Automation can check for updates but can never install one. See [Updates and installer](/umbra/docs/internals/updates-installer/).

:::note
Portable copies don't update themselves. **About** shows a download link instead.
:::

## Updating widgets and themes

Installed community widgets show an **Update** button on **Browse** when the catalog has a newer version. To update everything:

```powershell
umbractl update --all
```

A failure doesn't stop the rest; failures are listed in the result.

### Updates that ask for more

An update never grants new access silently. Umbra compares the new `widget.json` with the installed one and, if the update adds **hosts, system readings, media, notifications or commands**, it waits:

- **Settings** shows a box listing exactly what's new, and you accept or decline.
- `umbractl install <id>` refuses until you repeat it with `--accept-permissions`.
- `umbractl update --all` skips such widgets and lists them, so you accept them one by one.
- The MCP server strips `--accept-permissions`, so an agent can't approve for you.

The widget's `changelog` (if it has one) is shown with the request.

## Version numbers

Umbra and its tools share one version, from `Directory.Build.props`. Widgets and themes have their own `version`, bumped on every change; that's how Browse knows to offer an update.

---

# Troubleshooting

> Find out why a widget misbehaves, read logs, use safe mode and diagnostics, and understand what Umbra does when a widget crashes.

## Start here

1. **Is the widget enabled and visible?** Check **My widgets**: enabled, not hidden, and not limited by a time range or "only on AC power". The tray tooltip shows if edit mode or safe mode is on. Widgets also hide while a fullscreen app is in front if that option is on.
2. **Read the log.** `umbractl logs 100` prints the last lines (widget load errors, blocked network requests, crashes). The file is `%APPDATA%\Umbra\umbra.log`, and **Data & privacy → Open log** opens it. For more detail, set **General → Log level** to *verbose* (`umbractl general --log-level verbose`).
3. **Check blocked requests.** If a widget shows no data, **Data & privacy** lists requests it made to hosts it didn't declare. A widget can only reach HTTPS hosts listed in its `widget.json`.
4. **Try safe mode.** `umbractl safe-mode on` (or `Umbra.exe --safe`) closes all community widgets without deleting anything. If the problem goes away, turn widgets back on one at a time.

## Reporting a bug

**Settings → About → Copy diagnostics** (or `umbractl diagnostics`) produces a Markdown block with the Umbra version, Windows build, WebView2 version, monitors with DPI, GPU and proxy state, enabled widgets with versions and the last 30 log lines with your user paths hidden. It contains no option values, no proxy address and no widget data. Paste it into an [issue](https://github.com/AmineChr54/umbra/issues/new/choose); the link on the About page pre-fills your version.

## Common problems

**A widget stopped working.** If a widget's renderer exits unexpectedly, Umbra reloads it automatically, up to 3 times in 10 minutes. After that you see a host-drawn **"This widget stopped working"** page with a **Reload** button instead of a blank window. A hung renderer is only logged. If the whole WebView2 browser process exits, Umbra recreates it. Data & privacy shows each widget's crash count. See [Crash recovery](/umbra/docs/internals/crash-recovery/).

**A hotkey does nothing.** `umbractl hotkeys` shows each hotkey's status. `failed` includes the reason, most often that another app already owns that combination.

**Umbra says it's already running.** Only one instance runs per user (a portable copy has its own). A second launch opens Settings in the running copy instead. If you want to run from source, quit the installed Umbra first.

**WebView2 is missing.** Umbra needs the WebView2 runtime, which ships with current Windows. On startup Umbra checks for it and tells you if it's missing; install the Evergreen runtime from Microsoft.

**Widgets show "Offline".** The little status dot means the last fetches failed. Check your network or proxy (**General → Advanced → Proxy**).

**Everything is broken after a change.** **Data & privacy → Reset everything** returns Umbra to a clean state, or restore a [backup](/umbra/docs/using/data-privacy-backups/).

## For widget developers

`umbractl reload` re-scans widget folders after editing, `umbractl capture <id> out.png` shows exactly what the widget renders, and starting Umbra with `UMBRA_SIMULATE_OFFLINE=1` makes every host fetch fail so you can test the offline state. See [Testing with capture](/umbra/docs/widgets/testing/).

---

# Your first widget

> Scaffold, run, edit and screenshot a working widget in a few minutes, then see where to go next.

A widget is a folder with a `widget.json` and a web page. This walks through creating one, changing it and looking at the result. You need Umbra installed and a text editor; no build tools.

## 1. Scaffold it

```powershell
umbractl new my-widget
```

This writes a working widget into `%APPDATA%\Umbra\widgets\my-widget` and shows it on your desktop straight away. (Use `--name "My widget"` for a display name, or `--dir <folder>` to scaffold somewhere else; widgets outside the community folder aren't picked up until you load them with `umbractl create <folder>`.)

You now have:

```
my-widget/
  widget.json     the manifest
  index.html      the page
  style.css       styles
  main.js         the code
```

## 2. Read the manifest

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AmineChr54/umbra/main/schemas/widget.schema.json",
  "id": "my-widget",
  "name": "my-widget",
  "description": "Describe in one sentence why people want this widget.",
  "author": "your-github-name",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "entry": "index.html",
  "width": 260,
  "height": 120,
  "permissions": { "hosts": [] },
  "options": {
    "greeting": { "label": "Greeting", "type": "text", "default": "Hello" }
  }
}
```

`id` must equal the folder name. `width` and `height` are the widget's size in logical pixels. `permissions.hosts` is empty, so this widget can't reach the internet. `options` becomes a settings form on the widget's card in **My widgets**. The [manifest reference](/umbra/docs/widgets/manifest/) covers every field.

## 3. Read the page

`index.html` loads Umbra's stylesheet and SDK from the virtual host `umbra.local`, then your files:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://umbra.local/shared/umbra.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
...
<script src="https://umbra.local/shared/umbra.js"></script>
<script src="main.js"></script>
```

`umbra.css` gives you design tokens (colors, fonts, radii), and `umbra.js` gives you the global `umbra` object: options, refresh, data fetching, saved data and more. See [Page and lifecycle](/umbra/docs/widgets/page-and-lifecycle/).

## 4. Change it

Edit `main.js` or `style.css`, then tell Umbra to re-scan:

```powershell
umbractl reload
```

Change the option live without editing any file:

```powershell
umbractl set my-widget greeting "Good morning"
```

## 5. Fetch real data

To call an API, declare its host in `widget.json`, then use `umbra.fetchJson` inside `umbra.every`:

```json
"permissions": { "hosts": ["api.open-meteo.com"] }
```

```js
umbra.every(async () => {
  const data = await umbra.fetchJson("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=52.52&longitude=13.41&current=temperature_2m");
  document.getElementById("app").textContent = `${data.current.temperature_2m}°`;
  umbra.rendered();
});
```

Requests to any host you didn't declare are blocked, and `fetchJson` rejects. See the [JavaScript API](/umbra/docs/widgets/javascript-api/).

## 6. Look at it

```powershell
umbractl capture my-widget shot.png
```

This saves a PNG of just that widget and nothing else on screen. Check it at other sizes with `umbractl configure my-widget --scale 2`. [Testing with capture](/umbra/docs/widgets/testing/) has the full loop.

## 7. Make it good, then publish

Follow the [design guidelines](/umbra/docs/widgets/design-guidelines/) (true black background, tokens instead of hard-coded colors, tabular numbers), add a `preview.png`, and [publish it](/umbra/docs/widgets/publishing/) by pull request so it shows up in everyone's Browse page.

:::tip[Prefer to describe it?]
Connect an AI agent with `claude mcp add umbra -- umbractl mcp` and ask for the widget you want. The agent reads this documentation, writes the files, captures a screenshot and iterates. See [MCP server](/umbra/docs/automate/mcp/).
:::

---

# widget.json

> Every field of a widget manifest, option types, permissions and the rules Umbra validates.

Every widget has a `widget.json` in its folder. Umbra validates it when the widget loads, when it's installed, and in CI for catalog widgets (`node scripts/catalog.mjs`). Add the `$schema` line and your editor validates and completes it as you type:

```json
"$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AmineChr54/umbra/main/schemas/widget.schema.json"
```

## Example

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AmineChr54/umbra/main/schemas/widget.schema.json",
  "id": "weather",
  "name": "Weather",
  "description": "Current temperature and conditions for one city.",
  "author": "your-github-name",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "entry": "index.html",
  "preview": "preview.png",
  "width": 300,
  "height": 160,
  "defaultPosition": { "x": 24, "y": 420 },
  "permissions": { "hosts": ["api.open-meteo.com"] },
  "options": {
    "city":     { "label": "City", "type": "text", "default": "Berlin", "hint": "Shown under the field" },
    "units":    { "label": "Units", "type": "select", "default": "c",
                  "choices": [{ "value": "c", "label": "Celsius" }, { "value": "f", "label": "Fahrenheit" }] },
    "decimals": { "label": "Decimals", "type": "number", "default": 0, "min": 0, "max": 2, "step": 1 },
    "compact":  { "label": "Compact mode", "type": "toggle", "default": false }
  }
}
```

## Fields

| Field | Rules |
|---|---|
| `id` | Equals the folder name. 2 to 40 characters: lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter or digit (`^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{1,39}$`). |
| `name`, `description`, `author` | Required, non-empty. |
| `version` | Required, like `1.2.3`. **Bump it on every change**: it's how users get an Update button. |
| `changelog` | Optional, up to 500 characters: what changed. Shown when an update asks for new access and carried in the catalog index. |
| `entry` | The page to open. Default `index.html`. |
| `preview` | Screenshot for Browse. Recommended: a 2x capture on a black background. |
| `icon` | Optional tab icon for [tab groups](/umbra/docs/using/copies-and-tab-groups/): a 64×64 PNG, light grey on transparent. |
| `width`, `height` | Integers 80 to 1200, in **logical** pixels. Umbra scales them for the display's DPI and the user's size setting. |
| `defaultPosition` | `{ "x", "y" }` from the top left of the primary work area, in logical pixels. Omit to start at the top right. |
| `themeable` | Default `true`. `false` keeps your own look and ignores the user's [theme](/umbra/docs/using/appearance/). |
| `options` | The settings form in **My widgets**, in this order. See below. |
| `permissions` | What the widget may reach. See below. |

## Options

| `type` | Extra fields | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | `hint` | string |
| `number` | `min`, `max`, `step` | number |
| `select` | `choices`: a list of `{ "value", "label" }` (required) | the chosen `value` |
| `toggle` | none | boolean |

Every option has a `label` and a `default`. Read values in the page from `umbra.options`; they update live through `umbra.onSettings`. Users (and scripts) can change them with `umbractl set <id> <option> <value>`, which types the value by the schema.

## Permissions

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `hosts` | Every HTTPS hostname the widget may reach. **All other requests are blocked** (fetch, XHR, images, scripts, fonts). Use `[]` for offline widgets. |
| `notifications` | `true` to use `umbra.notify`. The user must also switch "Allow notifications" on for the widget in Settings (off by default). |
| `media` | `"read"` (`umbra.media.nowPlaying`) and/or `"control"` (`umbra.media.control`). |
| `system` | Any of `"cpu"`, `"memory"`, `"network"`, `"gpu"`, `"disk"`, for `umbra.system()` (`gpu` and `disk` need an Umbra newer than 1.14.0). |
| `commands` | Local programs the widget may start with `umbra.run`. Every command needs your approval. See [Running local commands](/umbra/docs/widgets/local-commands/). |

Browse shows every permission on the widget's card, and an update that adds any of them needs the user's approval. See [Sandbox and permissions](/umbra/docs/widgets/sandbox/).

## Files

A widget folder may contain `.html .js .mjs .css .svg .png .jpg .webp .gif .woff .woff2 .ttf .otf .json .txt .md` files, 5 MB in total. File paths must be relative with forward slashes and no `..`. See [widget.json schema](/umbra/docs/reference/widget-schema/) for the machine-readable definition, and the [SDK reference](/umbra/docs/widgets/sdk-reference/) for the full details in one page.

---

# Page and lifecycle

> How a widget page loads, when umbra.every runs, how settings and the paused state reach your code, and how drag, focus and zoom behave.

## The page

A widget page is plain HTML. Load Umbra's stylesheet and SDK from the virtual host `umbra.local`:

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://umbra.local/shared/umbra.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>
<body>
  <main id="app"></main>
  <script src="https://umbra.local/shared/umbra.js"></script>
  <script src="main.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
```

Your own files load relative to the page from `https://community.umbra.local/<id>/`. Pages can only load from Umbra's virtual hosts, `data:` and `blob:`, plus hosts declared in the manifest.

## The lifecycle

1. **Load.** The window opens with the true-black background. `umbra.js` asks the host for this widget's settings.
2. **`umbra.ready`** resolves when the host has sent them. `umbra.options`, `umbra.settings` and `umbra.widget` are then filled in.
3. **`umbra.every(fn)`** runs `fn` once ready and then every `refreshSeconds` (the user's setting, 30 to 600 s, or the widget's own interval). Errors are caught and logged.
4. **`umbra.rendered()`** is what you call after the first real frame is drawn; screenshots wait for it.
5. **Changes.** `umbra.onSettings(fn)` runs whenever the user changes anything: options, size, accent, locale, edit mode, the paused state.

```js
umbra.every(async () => {
  const { city } = umbra.options;
  const geo = await umbra.fetchJson(`https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=52.52&longitude=13.41&current=temperature_2m`);
  document.getElementById("app").textContent = `${city}: ${geo.current.temperature_2m}°`;
  umbra.rendered();
});
umbra.onSettings(() => { /* options changed: re-render without refetching if you can */ });
```

## When `umbra.every` runs

Besides the interval, it is also run on **Refresh all**, after the PC resumes from sleep, when the network comes back and after a long lock, at most once per 10 seconds. It does not run while `umbra.settings.paused` is true (PC locked or display off) and runs once when that ends. When Windows Energy Saver is on and the user allows slowing down, `refreshSeconds` is already 4x longer.

If you run your own timers or fetch loops, stop them while `umbra.settings.paused` is true, restart with one refresh when it turns false, and use `umbra.settings.refreshSeconds` as the interval so Energy Saver slows you down too.

## Several copies

Users can run a widget more than once. Each copy is a separate window with its own options, position, size and `umbra.store` data, so your code needs no extra work: read `umbra.options` and `umbra.store` as usual. Don't use `localStorage` for per-widget state (copies share it), and use `umbra.widget.instance` only if you must tell copies apart (`"<id>"` for the first copy, `"<id>#2"`, `"<id>#3"` for the rest).

## Time changes

When the clock or time zone changes, `new Date()` is right immediately, but anything you computed earlier (a countdown target, "today") is stale. Recompute in `umbra.onTimeChanged`, and schedule one timer for the next local midnight instead of polling:

```js
let midnight;
function scheduleMidnight() {
  clearTimeout(midnight);
  const now = new Date();
  const next = new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate() + 1);
  midnight = setTimeout(() => { render(); scheduleMidnight(); }, next - now + 50);
}
umbra.onTimeChanged(() => { render(); scheduleMidnight(); });
scheduleMidnight();
```

## Dragging

Holding the mouse button and moving more than 4 px drags the window (unless the user locked it). Put `data-no-drag` on buttons and links that need normal clicks. Inputs, textareas, selects and `contenteditable` elements never start a drag.

## Typing and focus

Widgets never take focus from the app you're using. Pressing the mouse on a text field gives the widget the keyboard; Umbra checks that a mouse button is physically down over the widget. If you create an input in code (say, rename on double-click), call `umbra.requestFocus()` first. `widgets/todo` is an example.

## Size, zoom and edit mode

Users can resize any widget from 50 % to 300 % of its manifest size. Umbra zooms the page like a browser, so layout in CSS pixels and let the page fill its window (`height: 100%`, flex, grid, `%` and `fr`) so extra room gets used. `devicePixelRatio` includes the zoom: canvas code that sizes its backing store by it stays crisp, and should redraw on `umbra.onSettings` when `umbra.settings.scale` changes. Don't scale the page yourself. In edit mode Umbra covers unlocked widgets with an overlay, so don't rely on mouse interaction then (`umbra.settings.editMode` tells you).

The full list of calls is in the [JavaScript API](/umbra/docs/widgets/javascript-api/).

---

# JavaScript API

> The window.umbra object by task - settings, fetching, saving data, notifications, media, system readings, formatting and utilities.

`umbra.js` adds one global, `window.umbra`. This page groups it by what you want to do. The one-table reference is in the [SDK reference](/umbra/docs/widgets/sdk-reference/#javascript-api-windowumbra).

## Know your settings

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `umbra.ready` | Promise that resolves when the host has sent this widget's settings. |
| `umbra.options` | This widget's option values, e.g. `{ city: "Berlin", units: "c" }`. |
| `umbra.settings` | `{ refreshSeconds, animations, locked, scale, locale, hour12, editMode, paused, energySaver, options }`, plus `accent` and `themeCss`. |
| `umbra.widget` | `{ id, instance, name }`: the widget (the folder) and this copy. |
| `umbra.onSettings(fn)` | Called with the new settings whenever the user changes anything. |
| `umbra.every(fn)` | Calls `fn` once ready, then every `refreshSeconds`. See [Page and lifecycle](/umbra/docs/widgets/page-and-lifecycle/). |
| `umbra.onTimeChanged(fn)` | Runs when the system clock or time zone changes. |

## Fetch data

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `umbra.fetchJson(url)` | `GET` JSON through the host: no CORS issues, 25 s timeout. Rejects unless the URL is HTTPS and its host is in `permissions.hosts`. |
| `umbra.fetchText(url)` | Like `fetchJson` but resolves the body as a string (up to 2 MB), for Markdown, CSV or HTML. |
| `umbra.status` | Data freshness (`state`, `lastOk`, `failures`, `ok()`, `failed()`, `onChange()`). See [Freshness and offline](/umbra/docs/widgets/offline/). |

Plain `fetch()` also works for declared hosts if the server allows CORS; `umbra.fetchJson` always works.

## Save data

```js
const tasks = await umbra.store.get("tasks", []);
tasks.push({ title: "Read chapter 3" });
await umbra.store.set("tasks", tasks);
umbra.store.onChange(async () => render(await umbra.store.get("tasks", [])));
```

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `umbra.store.get(key, fallback?)` | The saved value for `key` (any JSON), or `fallback`. |
| `umbra.store.set(key, value)` | Saves a JSON value. Rejects when the widget's data would pass 1 MB. |
| `umbra.store.remove(key)`, `umbra.store.keys()` | Delete a key; list the keys. |
| `umbra.store.onChange(fn)` | `fn(key)` when the data was changed from outside (`umbractl data`, MCP). `key` is `null` when everything was cleared. |

Use options for what the user picks, and `umbra.store` for what the widget creates. The store is private to the widget, survives restarts and updates, and lives in `%APPDATA%\Umbra\data\<id>.json`. Don't use `localStorage`: every widget shares one origin.

## Talk to the user and the system

| API | Needs | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `umbra.notify({ title, body?, url?, tag?, actions? })` | `permissions.notifications` and the user's switch | A real Windows toast. Up to 2 `actions`, `tag` replaces an earlier toast, 5 per 10 minutes per widget. A toast `url` must be HTTPS on a declared host. |
| `umbra.onNotificationAction(fn)` | | `fn({ id, tag })` when a toast button is clicked, while the widget is open. |
| `umbra.media.nowPlaying()` | `media: "read"` | The current Windows media session (`title`, `artist`, `album`, `app`, `status`, `playing`, `art?`…) or `null`. |
| `umbra.media.control(cmd)` | `media: "control"` | `play`, `pause`, `toggle`, `next`, `previous`. Needs a physical click on the widget in the last 2 s. |
| `umbra.system()` | `permissions.system` | `cpu.percent`, `memory.{totalBytes,usedBytes,percent}`, `network.{downBytesPerSec,upBytesPerSec}`, `gpu.{percent,memoryUsedBytes}`, `disk.{activePercent,readBytesPerSec,writeBytesPerSec,drives}`. Call from `umbra.every` or a short timer of your own. |
| `umbra.run(id, params?)` | `permissions.commands` | Runs a declared, user-approved command. See [Running local commands](/umbra/docs/widgets/local-commands/). |

## Format for the user's locale

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `umbra.locale` | The user's Windows region format as a BCP-47 tag (`"de-DE"`). Pass it to `Intl.*` and `toLocale*String`. |
| `umbra.hour12` | `true` when Windows uses a 12-hour clock. Pass it as `hour12`, and let an option override it if you offer one. |
| `umbra.fmt(n, decimals = 2)` | `7744.06` → `"7,744.06"`, or `"7.744,06"` when Windows is set to German. |

## Utilities

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `umbra.rendered()` | Call once the first real frame is drawn; screenshots wait for it. |
| `umbra.tween(from, to, ms, onFrame)` | Ease-out-cubic number animation; jumps to `to` when motion is off or the window is hidden. |
| `umbra.openUrl(url)` | Opens an http(s) link in the user's browser. Links never navigate the widget. |
| `umbra.requestFocus()` | Ask for the keyboard, only honoured right after a mouse press on the widget. |

:::tip
Widgets that must run on an older installed Umbra than the SDK they were written against should guard newer calls, for example `umbra.status?.failed(err)`.
:::

---

# Styling and tokens

> The design tokens in umbra.css, how themes and user appearance settings reach your widget, motion, and Windows contrast themes.

`https://umbra.local/shared/umbra.css` gives every widget the same foundation: the Segoe UI Variable font stack, tabular numbers (`.num`) and a set of design tokens. **Use the tokens instead of hard-coded colors**, so the user's theme and appearance settings restyle your widget.

## Tokens

| Token | Default | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `--bg` | `#000` | Window background |
| `--surface-1`, `--surface-2`, `--surface-3` | `#0a0a0c`, `#111114`, `#17171c` | Cards and raised areas |
| `--line`, `--line-strong` | white at 7 % / 12 % | Hairlines and borders |
| `--text`, `--text-2`, `--text-3` | `#f4f5f7`, `#a3a7b1`, `#6b707b` | Primary, secondary and muted text |
| `--accent`, `--accent-strong`, `--accent-soft` | `#8b93ff`, `#a9afff`, 14 % accent | Highlights, active states, glows |
| `--up`, `--down`, `--flat` | `#2fd58b`, `#ff5a5f`, `#9aa0aa` | Rising, falling and unchanged values |
| `--radius-s`, `--radius-m`, `--radius-l` | `8px`, `12px`, `18px` | Corner radii |

Read [`shared/umbra.css`](https://github.com/AmineChr54/umbra/blob/main/shared/umbra.css) for the complete list.

```css
.card { background: var(--surface-1); border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: var(--radius-m); }
.delta.up   { color: var(--up); }
.delta.down { color: var(--down); }
```

## Themes and user settings

The host turns the active [theme](/umbra/docs/themes/build-a-theme/) into one `:root { ... }` rule, which `umbra.js` applies after `umbra.css`. A widget that uses tokens follows the theme live. Set `"themeable": false` in the manifest to opt out.

On top of that, the user can set:

- a **corner radius** (overrides `--radius-s/m/l`),
- an **accent color** (`--accent`, `--accent-strong`, `--accent-soft`, also `umbra.settings.accent`; empty means the theme, "Match Windows accent" follows the system),
- **light text** (brighter `--text*`),
- an **interface font** (`--font`, `--font-display`) and **text size** (`--font-scale`, applied to the base font size, so use `em`/`rem` to follow it),
- a window **border**, and **reduce transparency** (solid `--line*` and `--accent-soft`; avoid translucent colors of your own if you want to honor it).

## Motion

`<html data-motion="on|off">` reflects the user's Animations setting and Windows' reduced-motion preference, and `umbra.css` turns off CSS animations when it's `off`. **Calm** animation speed sets `--motion-scale: 2`; multiply your durations:

```css
.panel { transition: opacity calc(200ms * var(--motion-scale, 1)); }
```

`umbra.tween` skips straight to the end value when motion is off.

## Windows contrast themes

When Windows has a contrast theme on, the page runs with `forced-colors: active`. Windows replaces colors and drops `box-shadow`s and most backgrounds, and `umbra.css` maps the tokens to system colors (`Canvas`, `CanvasText`, `Highlight`; `--up`, `--down` and `--flat` all become `CanvasText`), ignoring theme tokens. To stay readable:

- draw borders and separators with `border` or `outline`, not shadows,
- don't rely on color alone: give a rising or falling value the `trend-up` or `trend-down` class and `umbra.css` adds ▲ or ▼ in front of it (only in that mode),
- use `forced-color-adjust: none` only for things that must keep their own colors, such as a chart, and pick system colors yourself then.

## Sizing

Layout in CSS pixels and let the page fill its window. Users can resize a widget freely, and Umbra zooms the page; see [Page and lifecycle](/umbra/docs/widgets/page-and-lifecycle/#size-zoom-and-edit-mode). Follow the [design guidelines](/umbra/docs/widgets/design-guidelines/) for the house style.

---

# Freshness and offline

> How umbra.status tracks whether your widget's data is live, stale or offline, and how to show it.

A widget that fetches should tell the user when its numbers are old. The SDK does the bookkeeping, so every widget looks the same.

![Live, stale and offline states of the status dot](/umbra/img/umbra-status.png)

## How it works

- Every `umbra.fetchJson` / `umbra.fetchText` outcome is recorded; HTTP errors and timeouts are failures. There's nothing to call.
- `umbra.status.state` is:
  - `live` after a success,
  - `stale` when the data is older than 3× the refresh interval,
  - `offline` after two failures in a row, or a failure when nothing has loaded since the widget started,
  - `none` until the first fetch finishes.
- `<html data-stale>` is set while the state is `stale` or `offline`. Dim your numbers with CSS (keep it to `opacity`):

```css
html[data-stale] .price { opacity: 0.55; }
```

## The status dot

`<umbra-status></umbra-status>` is an optional element, styled by `umbra.css` with tokens: a small dot (`--up` live, `--text-3` stale, a ring when offline). Hovering it shows "Updated 3 min ago"; offline keeps "Offline · last data 10:42" visible. Put it in a footer, and use `placement="below-end"` in a top-right header so the hover text opens downwards. It's hidden while the state is `none`.

## Overriding the bookkeeping

- `umbra.status.failed(err)` for a response you can't use (a fetch's own Error is only counted once).
- `umbra.status.ok(new Date(savedAt))` to show data restored from `umbra.store` as "last data" at startup.
- `umbra.status.onChange(fn)` calls `fn(state)` when the state changes.

## Testing the offline state

Start Umbra from a shell with `UMBRA_SIMULATE_OFFLINE=1`; every host fetch then fails:

```powershell
$env:UMBRA_SIMULATE_OFFLINE = 1
dotnet run --project src/Umbra      # or start the installed Umbra.exe from this shell
```

:::tip
A widget that may run on an older Umbra than its SDK should call `umbra.status?.failed(err)`.
:::

---

# Running local commands

> How a widget declares and runs a local program, the strict rules around it, and how the user's approval works.

Most widgets never need this. A widget that must start a program (a launcher, `claude -p "Hello"`, a script runner) declares each command in `widget.json`, and the page can only name a declared **id**. This is the one place a widget runs code outside the sandbox, so it is tightly constrained.

## Declare it

```json
"permissions": {
  "commands": [
    { "id": "wake", "run": ["claude", "-p", "Hello"], "description": "Starts the Claude usage window" },
    { "id": "ask",  "run": ["claude", "-p", "${prompt}", "--model", "${model}"],
      "params": { "prompt": { "maxLength": 300 }, "model": { "choices": ["haiku", "sonnet"] } },
      "timeoutSeconds": 90 }
  ]
}
```

## Run it

```js
const r = await umbra.run("wake");   // { exitCode, stdout, stderr, timedOut, truncated, durationMs }
await umbra.run("ask", { prompt: "Say hi", model: "haiku" });
```

## The rules

These are checked when the widget loads, by `scripts/catalog.mjs`, and on install. A violation stops the widget from loading.

- `run` is `[executable, ...arguments]`, **never a shell line**. The executable is a plain program name found on `PATH` (`claude`, `python`) or an absolute local path (`C:\Tools\app.exe`); no relative paths, no UNC. The page can't change it.
- Each argument is a literal, or exactly `"${name}"` for a declared parameter. A parameter can't be part of a longer string (`"--model=${m}"` is rejected), and the executable can't be a parameter.
- A parameter is a string, always supplied, at most `maxLength` characters (default 200, max 1000), without control characters, and **must not start with `-` or `/`** unless it's one of the fixed `choices`.
- If the executable is an interpreter (`cmd`, `powershell`, `pwsh`, `wscript`, `cscript`, `mshta`, `node`, `python`, `py`, `bash`, `sh`, `wsl`, `rundll32`, `regsvr32`, `msiexec`, or a `.ps1`/`.bat`/`.cmd`/`.vbs`/`.js` file), every parameter needs fixed `choices`; free text is refused when the widget loads. A parameter reaches the program as one single argument, so spaces and quotes in it can't add arguments.
- `.cmd`/`.bat` files only start for commands without parameters. `timeoutSeconds` is 1 to 120 (default 60).

## How it runs

The program runs as you, with no window, in `%APPDATA%\Umbra\data\run\<widget id>`, with a scrubbed environment (system variables and `PATH` only: no tokens, no `UMBRA_*`). It and its descendants run in a job object and are killed on timeout or when Umbra exits. At most 1 MB of stdout and of stderr is kept (`truncated` tells you). Calls fail while the widget is disabled, and a running command stops when the widget closes.

## The user approves every command

The first run shows an Umbra prompt with the **exact command line**. The approval is saved for this widget and this command, and is void as soon as the command changes or the resolved program file (its path or SHA-256) differs.

- A prompt only appears right after the user clicked the widget (so a button works; a background timer doesn't), at most every 20 seconds, and not after three refusals. It closes as a refusal after 2 minutes.
- Without an approval, a call rejects with a message you should show ("Approve it in Settings > My widgets").
- Users approve and revoke each command in **Settings → My widgets**, and Browse flags widgets that declare commands.
- **Automation can't approve.** `umbractl approvals` and the MCP `list_command_approvals` are read-only, and backups never contain approvals.

:::caution
Declaring a command makes your widget need a human review. Prefer fixed `choices` over free-text parameters, and keep descriptions honest: they're shown to the user.
:::

`widgets/script-runner` is a worked example of the user's own scripts (below).

## The user's own scripts

A widget that runs whatever the user wants sets `"userScripts": true` in `permissions`. Its card in **Settings > My widgets** then gets a **Your scripts** section where the user adds, edits and deletes scripts (PowerShell, Python, Bash or a program; a file, or code typed right there). The widget lists them with `umbra.commands()`, re-reads them in `umbra.onCommandsChange`, and runs them by id with `umbra.run`.

- Umbra builds the command (`powershell ... -File <script>`, `python <script>`, `bash <script>`, `<program>`), never a shell line, and the row in Settings shows it.
- Saving in Settings is the approval. Only Settings can add, change, delete or approve a script; no `umbractl` or MCP tool can, and the widget's page only sees ids and names.
- Scripts are kept outside the widget folder, so updating the widget keeps them. The same timeout, output cap and environment rules apply.
- An optional **Start in** folder sets where the script runs. Picking a Windows shortcut (`.lnk`) with Browse fills the file, arguments and Start in from it.
- **Keeps running** (a tunnel, a server, a watcher) is a choice in the editor: no time limit, only the last 64 KB of output kept, and it stops when the user presses Stop (widget, Settings or tray), when the widget closes, when the script is edited or deleted, and with Umbra. Optional: start automatically while the widget is on, and restart if it stops (5 tries with growing waits). Only the user's own scripts can keep running, never a command declared in `widget.json`.
- **Run as administrator** (scripts that run and finish only) is a switch in the editor. Each run shows Windows' own UAC prompt, only starts right after a click on the widget, returns its output like any other run (through a small PowerShell helper that Windows elevates), and is approved only in Settings. `widget.json` can't ask for it.
- `umbra.stop(id)` stops a run or a script that keeps running; `umbra.commandOutput(id)` returns what it printed so far, for live output.

---

# Sandbox and permissions

> What a widget can and cannot do, and the permissions that widen it.

Every widget runs in a WebView2 window with the host app watching its requests. The rules are the same for built-in, community and agent-written widgets.

## What a widget can do

- Load its own files from `community.umbra.local`, and Umbra's SDK and styles from `umbra.local`.
- Use `data:` and `blob:` URLs.
- Reach the HTTPS hosts listed in `permissions.hosts`, through `umbra.fetchJson` / `fetchText` (which avoids CORS) or plain `fetch` where the server allows it.
- Save data in its own `umbra.store` file (1 MB), and nothing else on disk.
- Open an http(s) link in your browser through `umbra.openUrl`.

## What a widget cannot do

- **Reach any other host.** Any other request, including images, scripts, fonts and XHR, gets an HTTP 403 from the host app. HTTP (non-TLS) is never allowed.
- **Navigate away or open windows.** Top-level navigation off the virtual hosts is cancelled, and links open in your browser.
- **Take focus.** It gets the keyboard only right after a physical mouse press on it.
- **Resize or zoom itself.** The page's resize and zoom messages are honoured only in edit mode, for an unlocked widget, with a physical mouse press (resize) or <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> held (zoom) over that window.
- **Use devtools or the browser context menu.** Right-click opens Umbra's own menu (Refresh, Options, Lock, Edit mode, Hide, Add another copy); a widget that calls `preventDefault()` on `contextmenu` keeps its own, and <kbd>Shift</kbd>+right-click always opens Umbra's. Browser zoom keys are off.
- **Touch the file system or the machine**, except through user-approved [commands](/umbra/docs/widgets/local-commands/).

## Permissions

| Permission | Lets the widget |
|---|---|
| `hosts` | Reach specific HTTPS hostnames |
| `notifications` | Show Windows toasts (and only if you switch notifications on for it) |
| `media` | Read (`"read"`) and/or control (`"control"`) the current media session |
| `system` | Read CPU, memory, network, GPU or disk totals |
| `commands` | Start specific local programs, each approved by you |

Browse shows every permission on each widget's card, and **Data & privacy** shows what each installed widget can reach and which requests were blocked.

## Updates can't widen it silently

An update to an installed catalog widget never grants new access on its own. Umbra compares the new manifest with the installed one (hosts, system, media, notifications, commands) and refuses until you accept. See [Updates](/umbra/docs/using/updates/#updates-that-ask-for-more). Files written by community installs and by agents are validated too: relative forward-slash paths only, no `..`, allowed extensions only, 5 MB, id equal to the folder, all staged in a temp folder and checked before they're committed.

## Why it matters when you build

- Declare **every** host you call, and no more: reviewers read this list.
- Prefer offline designs. `"hosts": []` is the easiest widget to approve.
- Don't ask for notifications, media, system or commands unless the widget's purpose needs it.

The deeper reasoning and the exact checks are in the [security model](/umbra/docs/internals/security/).

---

# Design guidelines

> The house style for Umbra widgets - true black, tokens, tabular numbers, calm motion and honest data - and how reviewers judge a widget.

Umbra widgets should look like they belong together on one desktop. These rules are what reviewers check.

## Look

- **True black background (`#000`)**, no transparency. Umbra is built for OLED, where black pixels are off, and the window has DWM-drawn rounded corners and a hairline border.
- **Use the tokens** for every color, radius and font (`var(--text)`, `var(--accent)`, `var(--radius-m)`), so themes work. See [Styling and tokens](/umbra/docs/widgets/styling/).
- **Segoe UI Variable** comes from `umbra.css`; don't ship your own fonts unless the widget is about typography.
- **Text 11 px or larger.** Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` (the `.num` class) for numbers that change, so they don't jitter.
- Fit the declared `width` × `height` exactly. The window doesn't scroll or reflow; when the user resizes it, Umbra zooms the whole page. Let the page fill its window (`height: 100%`, flex, grid) so extra room gets used.

## Motion

- **Calm by default.** No constant animation. A short entrance and meaningful transitions are fine.
- Respect `html[data-motion="off"]` (`umbra.css` already disables CSS animations there) and multiply durations by `var(--motion-scale, 1)`.
- Use `umbra.tween` for number animations, since it jumps to the end value when motion is off or the window is hidden.

## Data and behavior

- **No network calls faster than `umbra.every` schedules them.** If you run your own timers, stop them while `umbra.settings.paused` is true and use `umbra.settings.refreshSeconds` as the interval.
- **Show freshness.** Dim stale numbers and put an `<umbra-status>` in the footer. See [Freshness and offline](/umbra/docs/widgets/offline/).
- **Format for the user's region** with `umbra.locale`, `umbra.hour12` and `umbra.fmt`, not a hard-coded `"en-US"`.
- **Save what the widget creates** in `umbra.store`, never in `localStorage`.
- **Handle edit mode and locking.** Don't rely on mouse interaction while `umbra.settings.editMode` is true; mark buttons `data-no-drag` so clicks stay clicks.
- Recompute anything derived from "today" in `umbra.onTimeChanged`.

## Accessibility

- Give controls real labels, and keep contrast readable on your surfaces.
- Don't rely on color alone for rising or falling values: add the `trend-up` / `trend-down` classes so Windows contrast themes get ▲ and ▼.
- Draw borders with `border`/`outline`, not `box-shadow`, so they survive forced-colors mode.

## Honest permissions

- Declare **only** the hosts the widget calls, and only the permissions its purpose needs.
- Prefer designs that work offline.
- If you need a local command, read [Running local commands](/umbra/docs/widgets/local-commands/) first; it makes review stricter.

## Before you open a pull request

- [ ] `widget.json` has a clear one-sentence `description`, a `version`, and `$schema`.
- [ ] A 2× `preview.png` on a black background (`umbractl capture <id> preview.png`).
- [ ] No hard-coded colors; checked at 50 %, 100 % and 200 % size.
- [ ] Checked with animations off and with the offline simulation.
- [ ] `node scripts/catalog.mjs` passes and `widgets/index.json` is regenerated.

---

# Testing with capture

> The develop-capture-fix loop with umbractl, including pixel-exact screenshots, sizes, simulated offline, logs and testing the catalog locally.

The fastest way to build a widget is a tight loop: change a file, reload, **look at the result**, repeat. `umbractl` (installed with Umbra) makes that loop scriptable, and it's the same loop an AI agent uses over MCP.

## The loop

```powershell
umbractl new my-widget                  # scaffold a working widget and show it
umbractl create .\widgets\my-widget     # (re)load a folder you are editing elsewhere, e.g. in the repo
umbractl reload                         # re-scan widget folders after editing files in place
umbractl capture my-widget shot.png     # PNG of just that widget
umbractl logs                           # load errors and requests blocked by the sandbox
```

If your widget lives in `%APPDATA%\Umbra\widgets\my-widget`, run `umbractl reload` after each edit. If you're editing in a repo checkout, load it with `umbractl create <folder>`.

## Capture

`umbractl capture <id|settings:page> [file.png]` writes a pixel-exact PNG of one surface: a widget (by id, or `sp500#2` for a copy) or a Settings page (`settings:general`, `widgets`, `layouts`, `browse`, `themes`, `hotkeys`, `privacy`, `about`). It captures only that WebView, never the rest of your screen, and waits for your widget to call `umbra.rendered()`. A 2× capture on black is exactly what Browse wants as `preview.png`.

:::tip
Look at the PNG. Don't assume a change worked because the code ran.
:::

## Try states and sizes

```powershell
umbractl set my-widget city Paris            # an option value, typed by the schema
umbractl configure my-widget --scale 2       # how it looks at 200 % (back with --scale 1)
umbractl configure my-widget --scale 0.5     # and at 50 %
umbractl general --animation-speed off       # motion off
umbractl data my-widget                      # what the widget saved with umbra.store
umbractl data my-widget tasks '[{"title":"x"}]'   # set a key to test restore paths
umbractl privacy my-widget                   # hosts, commands, saved data, blocked requests
```

For the offline state, start Umbra from a shell with `UMBRA_SIMULATE_OFFLINE=1`: every host fetch fails, so you can check what your widget shows when data is old.

## Check the sandbox

`umbractl logs` lists blocked requests. If your widget calls a host it didn't declare, you'll see the 403 there and in **Data & privacy**; add the host to `permissions.hosts` only if the widget really needs it.

## Test the catalog end to end

To test the Browse page with your local repo, point Umbra at it:

```powershell
$env:UMBRA_CATALOG_BASE = "file:///C:/path/to/umbra/widgets"
node scripts/catalog.mjs          # validates and rebuilds widgets/index.json and themes/index.json
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\Umbra\Umbra.exe"
```

## Through an AI agent

An MCP client does the same with `create_widget`, `configure_widget`, `widget_data`, `read_logs` and `capture`; see [MCP server](/umbra/docs/automate/mcp/).

---

# Publishing to the catalog

> Get your widget into everyone's Browse page with one pull request, and what review and CI check.

The catalog is this repository's `widgets/` folder. Publishing a widget is one pull request.

## Steps

1. **Fork and clone** the repository (`gh repo fork AmineChr54/umbra --clone`) and create a branch.
2. **Add `widgets/<id>/`** with your files: `widget.json`, the entry page, code and styles, and a 2× `preview.png` (`umbractl capture <id> preview.png`). Add `icon.png` if you want a tab icon.
3. **Run the catalog tool** and commit the result:
   ```powershell
   node scripts/catalog.mjs
   ```
   This validates your widget and regenerates `widgets/index.json` (and `themes/index.json`). **Never edit the index by hand.**
4. **Open a pull request** that adds only `widgets/<id>/` and the regenerated index.

If another widget PR lands first and your index conflicts, rebase on `main` and run `node scripts/catalog.mjs` again.

## What CI checks

CI runs `node scripts/catalog.mjs --check`, which fails the PR if the committed index is stale (nothing regenerates or commits it after the merge). Validation covers the id, the required fields, the semantic version, the hostnames, the option types, the command rules, the file types and the 5 MB limit.

## What reviewers check

- The widget only uses the hosts it declares, and the permissions match its purpose.
- It looks at home next to the others: see the [design guidelines](/umbra/docs/widgets/design-guidelines/).
- It's honest: description, preview and behavior match.
